4. The defendant No.1 thereafter, filed an application under the provision of Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit to its file and number on the averments that without serving any summons and notice upon him, the plaintiff fraudulently obtained an ex parte decree against him and by that he sustained irreparable injury. It is also pleaded that he for the first time on 27-7-1986 got the knowledge that the plaintiff was getting deed of conveyance executed and registered with respect to the suit property. There having been a delay in filing the said application the defendant filed an application under the provision of section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of the said delay. The said application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code has been registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1986. 

 5. The plaintiff resisted the said Miscellaneous Case by presenting a written objection taking the stand that the defendant No.1 having been well aware of the institution of the Suit, on 17-1-1986 appeared in the Court and filed an application for time for presenting written statement. The defendant No.1 having not filed any written statement, the suit was decreed ex parte on 3-4-1985. The defendant No.1, thereafter, through his Advocate withdrew the money deposited in the Court by the plaintiff through Challan. The Miscellaneous Case stood barred by limitation, it is further alleged in the written objection. 

 7. The learned trial Judge on examination of the record found that the defendant No. 1 appeared in the court through a Vokalatnama and he signed on the same. The learned trial Judge on a comparison of the signature of the defendant appearing on the deposition in the Miscellaneous case and the Vokalatnama filed on 17-1-85 found that the two signatures were the product of same handwriting. The learned trial Judge, ultimately, came to the conclusion that the presence of the defendant in the Court on 17-1-85 and the withdrawal of the money is a proof that he had been well aware of the proceeding of the suit since 17-1-85 and the Miscellaneous case stood barred by limitation. With the above finding, the learned trial Judge dismissed the Miscellaneous Case. 

 8. The defendant-petitioner, against the said decision of the learned trial Judge carried an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 26 of 1989 to the learned District Judge, Kushtia. The learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat heard the appeal. The learned Subordinate Judge recorded the following findings: 

 (iv) It appeared that both the defendants appeared on off date and in both the cases the Sheristadar-in-Charge sitting in the Sheresta allowed the applications on behalf of the presiding judge; 

 (5) The learned Munsif committed a serious error of law in holding that the Miscellaneous Case is barred by limitation inasmuch as the defendant-petitioner brought the Miscellaneous Case for setting aside the ex parte decree within stipulated period of limitation from the date of his knowledge. 

 "13. (1) In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may apply to the Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, the Court shall make on order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit : 

 15. Order IX, rule 13 mandates that in an application under rule 13 of Order IX the court has to satisfy itself, (a) the summons had not been duly served upon the defendant, or (b) the defendant has been prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing and if either of the conditions are satisfied, the court is bound to set aside the ex parte decree. In the case before me the first part of the Rule is relevant. 

 17. Keeping in view of the above provisions of law let me now see whether the summons and also the registered notice has been duly served upon the defendant and also whether he could make out a case for setting aside the ex parte decree passed against him on the ground of non-service of summons upon him. 

 20. On a reading of the judgment of both the courts below it appears that both the courts below failed to appreciate the moot point which arose for their consideration in the resolution of the controversy. It has been already pointed out that under Order IX, rule 6 of the Code when the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not appear when the suit is called on for hearing then if it is proved that the summons was duly served meaning that service in such way as to give information of the suit to the defendant then only the court is empowered to proceed ex parte. The court must hold due service of summons proved and it is only then that it can award an ex parte decree. The ex parte decree must be set aside where the court finds that the defendant was not duly served with the summons even if the defendant was aware of the institution of the suit against him. The learned trial Judge did not at all care to bear in mind the provisions contained in rules 6 and 13 of Order IX of the Code. The learned trial Judge laid stress on the fact of appearance of defendant No. 1 by a Vokalatnama praying for time for filing written statement and withdrawing the money deposited in the court by the plaintiff and thus committed an error in taking the view that the defendant was aware of the suit since 17-1-85 and the Miscellaneous case was barred by limitation. The learned trial Judge, thus, misdirected himself in his approach on the matter. The learned Artha Rin Adalat being the appellate Court recorded the positive finding that the service of summons upon the defendant had not been proved and also that there was no proof that the summons and the registered notice were ever issued upon the defendants. The lower appellate Court also recorded the finding that there had been procedural defect in the analysis and decision arrived at by the trial Court. In view of the recording of the above positive findings there was no alternative left for the lower appellate Court but to reverse the decision of the trial Court and restore the suit to its file and number on setting aside the ex parte decree thus allowing the Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code. The lower appellate Court failed to take notice that in a proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code if it is found that summons were not duly served upon the defendant that is sufficient for knocking down the ex parte decree. The Appellate Division in Abdur Rashid and another vs. Abdul Barik and another, 35 DLR (AD) 162 considered the nature and scope of the provision of Order IX rule 13 of the Code in setting aside an ex parte decree. The observations of their Lordships of the Appellate Division are couched in the following language : 

 "Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code, if summons is not duly served on the defendant, that is a good ground for setting aside an ex parte decree. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Code it would be apparent, that due service of summons is an essential condition, which must be satisfied before the Court can proceed to give a judgment and under Order IX, rule 13 if a party satisfies a Court that summons were not duly served upon him, the Court is bound to set aside an ex parte decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex parte decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of suit. No provision of law could be pointed out by the learned Counsel for the respondent, which dispenses with the necessity of proper service of summons." 

 21. Let me direct my attention to the contention raised by the plaintiff in the courts below that the defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit by executing a Vokalatnama engaging a learned Advocate praying for a time for presenting written statement and also for withdrawing the money deposited by the plaintiff in the court, though, this contention, is not at all material in disposing of a proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code for setting aside an ex parte decree on the ground of non-service of summons. In this context the allegation made by the defendant-petitioner may be looked into. It is the assertion of the defendant-petitioner that no summons and registered notice were ever served upon him and he did never appear in the suit by engaging any Advocate executing any Vokalatnama empowering the Advocate to do any act on his behalf in the suit. It is also asserted that he did not withdraw the money deposited in the court. In his evidence he gave testimony that in the suit no summons or notice had been served upon him and he did neither appear in the suit nor did engage any lawyer nor did pray for any time for filing written statement. He testified that the signature appearing in the Vokalatnama is not his signature. In the cross-examination he stated that he did not know Advocate Golam Mohammad and he denied the suggestion put forward by the plaintiff that he engaged Golam Mohammad as his lawyer. In view of this unequivocal testimony of the defendant-petitioner no attempt was made from the side of the plaintiff-opposite-party to have his signature appearing in the Vokalatnama and the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and also the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act compared with the signature appearing on the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-1985 filed in the suit by a Handwriting expert. The trial Court on a comparison of the signature of the defendant-petitioner appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the signature appearing in his deposition dated 24-5-87 found that both the signatures are the product of the same handwriting. On a scrutiny of the signature of the defendant-petitioner appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the signature appearing in his deposition dated 24-5-87 found that both the signatures are the product of the same handwriting. On a scrutiny of the signature of the defendant-petitioner appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 as well as the application for withdrawing the money deposited in the court it appears that the signature bears the name "Md Abu Zafor Mia" (মোঃ আবু জাফ মিয়া) On examination of the Vokalatnama dated 23-8-86 filed in the Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and the signature appearing on the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act and the deposition recorded in the Miscellaneous case it appears that the signature bears the name "Md Abu Zafor Sheikh (Mia) মোঃ আবু জাফর মিয়া শেখ (মিয়া) On a close scrutiny of the signatures of the defendant-petitioner appearing on the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the application for withdrawing the money dated 8-6-85 it cannot be said that the signature appearing in the said Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the application dated 8-6-85 and the signature appearing on the Vokalatnama and the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code as well as the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act and the deposition dated 14-5-1987 are the products of the same hand writing. The trial Court was not well founded in recording the finding that the signature appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-1985 and the signature appearing in the deposition dated 24-5-1987 are the product of the same handwriting. 

 While the meaning of the term "Court" will vary with the context in which it is used, generally speaking a Court is a body in the government to which the public administration of justice is delegated, being a tribunal officially assembled under authority of law, at the appropriate time and place, for the administration of justice, through which the state enforces its sovereign rights and powers, and consisting in its jurisdiction and functions and not its title or name, although in cases where the character of a Court as created is inconclusive the legislative label or name given to it may be a determining factor in ascertaining its character." 

 A Court is according to Coke on Littleton, a place where justice is judicially administered and justice is understood in the forensic world, to be a decision of a binding nature given on a point of dispute in a list between two or more contending parties, by applying the law of the land to the facts of the case, untrammelled by the subjective attitude of the decision making body in exercise of the judicial power of the state and by following a judicial procedure." 

 A Judge is a Public officer lawfully appointed to determine questions in dispute between the litigants upon merit according to law. A Judge is an officer who presides at a Court. "Judge" is defined in Anderson's Law Dictionary as a "public officer" whose function is to declare the law, to conduct the trial of cases between litigants according to legal force. 

 37. The Sheristadar is not a Public officer and his function is not to declare law and to conduct the trial of case between litigants and is not invested with any authority to determine any cause or question in a court of judicature created by any Act or Statute. The Sheristadar, as such, did not possess any judicial power to grant any time to the defendants and also to set down the Suit for ex parte hearing and all his orders and acts are absolutely without jurisdiction and the ex parte decree passed on the basis of the orders passed by the Sheristadar are also without jurisdiction. The ground so urged being very much substantial is accepted. 

 38. Turning now to the next ground which relates to the question of limitation, the learned trial Judge taking the view that since the defendant-petitioner appeared in the suit on 17-1-85 and withdrew the money on 16-8-1985, he was well aware of the proceeding of the suit since 17-1-85 and the Miscellaneous case for restoration of the suit having been filed after a long time, the same stood barred by limitation. The appellate Court did not come to any decision on the question of limitation. It has already been found that no summon was served upon the defendant. Elements of fraud and collusion has been also noticed in the matter of procuring ex parte decree by the plaintiff. The defendant in his application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code made averment that without serving any summons upon him, the plaintiff obtained a fraudulent ex parte decree and he sustained irreparable injury by the said decree and he on 27-7-86 came to know that the plaintiff was getting kabala deed executed and registered with respect to the suit land on the basis of a fraudulent ex parte decree passed in title Suit No. 385 of 1984. The defendant in his evidence also stated that no notice was served upon him and he did never appear in the suit by presenting a Vokalatnama and also engaging a lawyer. The plaintiff, though, in the written objection filed against the Miscellaneous case asserted that summons of the suit had been duly served upon him, the said assertion could not be established by any legal evidence. The lower appellate Court recorded the positive finding that it was not proved that summons was served. In an application for setting aside an ex parte decree on the ground of non-service of summons, Article 164 of the Limitation Act is attracted. Article 164 enjoins that by a defendant for an order to set aside a decree ex parte period of limitation is 30 days when the applicant has knowledge of the decree where the summons was not duly served. It appears from materials on record that the defendant for the first time on 27-7-86 got the knowledge of the ex parte decree and on 23-8-86 filed the Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code which was very much within 30 days of the date of knowledge of the ex parte decree, ie on 27-7-1986. My considered view is that the Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code has been filed within the period of 30 days of the date of knowledge and the same is not barred by limitation. 

 39. Let me now come to a legal aspect of the case. In the matter of getting an ex parte decree the plaintiff is bound to prove his case to the satisfaction of the Court and his burden is not lightened because the defendant is absent. This is so even when the defendant has lost the right to produce evidence. It is the duty of the court to consider the interest of the absentee defendant. The court in awarding an ex parte decree is to observe minimum legal requirements and the court is to apply its judicial mind as to whether the plaintiff by papers and witnesses proved his case. It is to be borne in mind that the absence of the defendant is no ground for passing an ex parte decree in favour of a plaintiff. In the case in my hand the plaintiff prayed for specific performance of contract on the basis of an unregistered agreement to sale deed (Bainanama) and the said deed is prescribed by one Mohani Mohan and attested by two witnesses, namely, Md Tamijuddin and Md Abdul Khaleque Khan. It appears that plaintiff only examined himself in support of his case and neither the scribe nor any of the attesting witnesses has been examined in support of the .execution of the agreement to sale deed (Bainanama). It was the duty of the plaintiff to prove the agreement to sale deed by examining the scribe and at least one of the said attesting witnesses of the said deed. It, thus, appears that minimum legal requirements were not at all followed in awarding an ex parte decree. The order also does not show that the court applied its judicial mind in awarding an ex parte decree, more so, when the decree is of a Specific Performance of Contract on the basis of an unregistered agreement to sale deed. The order awarding ex parte decree did not satisfy the minimum requirement of Order 20 rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The case of Bangladesh vs. Abdul Wadud and others, 25 DLR (SC) 90, Bangladesh vs. Israil Ali and others. 1981 BLD (AD) 371 and Nurjahan Begum vs. Giri Gopal Sarker being dead his heirs Dulal Chandra Sarker and another, 1979 BSCR 400 may be profitably referred to in this context. 

 40. The proposition of law emerging out of the above authorities is that in ex parte disposal of the Suit the Court is required to observe minimum legal requirement and the order should show application of the Court's judicial mind as to whether the plaintiff's witnesses and other papers produced proved the plaintiff's case. 

 41. The duty of a Court is to administer justice in accordance with law. Courts are required not to exercise punitive jurisdiction by depriving defendant ex parte. Our law of Procedure is also designed to facilitate justice and further its end. The laws of procedure are grounded on the principle that a litigant public and a citizen should not be condemned unheard, that decision should not be reached behind his back, that proceeding that affects his properties should not be deprived from participating in them. The Court possesses a discretion to undo injustice caused to the men, the public and the citizens of the State and the Court must exercise that discretion. The hands of the Court are not tied by the ex parte orders. Mandate of law is that interference must be called for in a given case and, if interference is not called for then it is not exercising the discretion which the law says it should. In this context it is significant to point out that in furtherance of the ends of justice court always leans in favour of setting aside an ex parte decree/order rather than maintaining the same because court exists for the advancement of justice and ordinarily would not be understood to deprive a litigant of his right. 

 43. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to cost, the judgments of the courts below are set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure arising out of Title Suit No. 385 of 1984 is allowed and the said Title Suit No. 385 of 1984 is restored to its file and number.
